Kiyi embryos incubated at 4 °C [T = 4 °C] exhibit an extended developmental period, with eclosion typically occurring after approximately 130 days [ab = approximately 130 days]. This protracted incubation phase, consistent with the slow embryogenesis of deepwater coregonines, produces yolk-sac larvae weighing roughly 0.006 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.006 grams]. These newly emerged prolarvae, often termed alevins, remain dependent upon their endogenous yolk reserves for several weeks, absorbing nutrients from their yolk sacs before initiating exogenous feeding. The low-temperature regime of their profundal spawning grounds imposes a metabolic constraint that decouples development from the more rapid schedules seen in littoral-zone congeners. This comparatively long incubation period, lasting from the fertilised ovum stage through chorion rupture, likely reflects both the thermal environment and the species' relatively large egg diameter of 2 to 3 mm from which the neonatal mass is computed.

As juvenile kiyi grow and approach reproductive maturation, a distinct body size threshold marks the transition to puberty. Field surveys and laboratory rearing studies indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 13.2 centimetres [Lp = approximately 13.2 centimetres], at which point individuals typically attain a wet weight at puberty of about 24.5 grams [Wwp = about 24.5 grams]. This weight corresponds well with the ontogenetic scaling relationships derived from length-mass regressions for this species. The onset of gonadal activity and vitellogenesis in females, along with spermiation in males, occurs once this size criterion is met, though the exact age at which this happens can vary considerably depending on local trophic conditions. In the oligotrophic waters of the Great Lakes, where prey densities can be low, the growing juvenile may take several additional years to reach this pubertal milestone compared to conspecifics in more productive environments. Puberty therefore appears linked more tightly to body size than to chronological age in this species.

Under typical thermal conditions in the hypolimnion, where summer temperatures hover near 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the maximum reproduction rate is achieved through a combination of moderate fecundity per spawning event and annual iteroparity. Mature females produce approximately 145 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 145 eggs per spawning event], and can complete a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = a single spawning event each year], yielding a substantial lifetime reproductive output. This annual broadcast spawning strategy, involving the release of demersal adhesive eggs over cobble substrates, is typical of deepwater coregonines that exhibit capital breeding, relying on stored lipids accumulated during the preceding summer and autumn to fuel gametogenesis. The peak spawning period in the Great Lakes occurs during late autumn and early winter, with gravid females descending from their pelagic feeding grounds to traditional reef spawning sites. The exact timing of spawning is synchronised by photoperiod and temperature cues, ensuring that egg deposition occurs when predation risk from benthic fishes is minimal.

The maximum recorded total length for kiyi reaches approximately 35 centimetres [Li = approximately 35 centimetres], with the largest individuals attaining an ultimate wet weight of around 565 grams [Wwi = around 565 grams]. These asymptotic dimensions are among the more modest within the Coregonus genus, reflecting the species' adaptation to the cold, low-productivity waters of the Great Lakes basin. Males and females exhibit minimal sexual size dimorphism, though gravid females in the weeks prior to spawning can appear noticeably heavier due to their developing ovaries. The length-weight relationship, described by the power function W = 0.00603 L^3.22, indicates a slightly positive allometric growth pattern, meaning that larger individuals are proportionally heavier than would be predicted by isometric scaling. This allometry likely reflects the accumulation of visceral lipid reserves essential for overwintering survival and reproductive provisioning. Annual growth increments decline markedly after sexual maturation, with the majority of somatic growth occurring during the first three to four years of life.

Maximum lifespan in the wild, based on otolith annuli from the oldest documented individuals, reaches approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C], a longevity that positions the kiyi as a relatively slow-paced species among Great Lakes coregonines. This decelerated life-history strategy, featuring delayed maturity coupled with extended reproductive tenure, stands in contrast to the faster-paced semelparous life cycles of many Pacific salmonids. Senescent adults during their final year exhibit reduced body condition, thinning of the visceral fat deposits, and a progressive deterioration of ovarian function, culminating in post-reproductive mortality. The species' natural mortality rates are highest during the egg and early larval stages, when predation from deepwater sculpins and burbot exacts a heavy toll, but adult mortality rates remain low and relatively constant across the 3-to-10 year age window. Understanding this lifespan constraint is critical for population viability models.
